original_question: When can a non-trivial virtual knot arise as the connected sum of two trivial virtual knots? Equivalently, for long virtual knots whose closure is the unknot, classify which non-isotopic long virtual knots can close to the same trivial compact knot and thereby explain when different connected-sum choices for closed virtual knots can produce a non-trivial result.
target_in_paper: Section 8.1, Problem 1 ("Recognizing the Kishino knot"): the classification problem asking when a non-trivial virtual knot can occur as a connected sum of two trivial virtual knots, together with the paper's closely related reformulation in terms of long virtual knots whose closures are the unknot.
correct_elements: Your draft captures the central problem in the paper very well: it asks for a classification of non-trivial virtual knots that arise as connected sums of two trivial virtual knots, and it correctly brings in the long-virtual-knot viewpoint and the role of closure to the unknot. Those are exactly the ingredients emphasized in the paper's discussion of the Kishino phenomenon.
missing_details: The nearest official formulation is explicitly in Section 8.1, Problem 1, under the heading "Recognizing the Kishino knot"; the Kishino diagram is the motivating example for the question.
The paper does not state that the long-knot formulation is equivalent to the connected-sum question; it states only that it is closely related.

A stand-alone version should distinguish closed (compact) virtual knots from long virtual knots: connected sum for closed virtual knots is not well defined, while for long virtual knots it is ordered and well defined.
The relevant closure operation is the natural map from long virtual knots to oriented compact virtual knots obtained by joining the two ends.

The long-knot side should be phrased as classifying different long virtual knots whose closures are equivalent to the unknot, not merely as an arbitrary same-closure classification without reference to the unknot.

It helps to state the motivating examples supplied earlier in the paper: the parts of the Kishino knot close to unknots, and Section 5.2 gives an explicit example showing that a non-trivial virtual diagram can be a connected sum of two trivial virtual diagrams.

No ambient ring, field, degree, homogeneity, or nilpotency hypotheses are involved here; the hidden assumptions are categorical/topological ones about long versus closed virtual knots and the closure map.
refined_question: Motivated by the Kishino diagram, classify precisely when a non-trivial closed virtual knot can be obtained as a connected sum of two trivial virtual knots. Since connected sum of closed virtual knots is not well defined, analyze this through the ordered, well-defined connected sum on long virtual knots by determining which distinct long virtual knots have closures equivalent to the unknot, and how different choices of long representatives can produce a non-trivial closed virtual knot after closure.
justification: The paper's exact target is the question stated in Section 8.1, Problem 1, where the authors say that the non-triviality of the Kishino diagram despite its decomposition into trivial summands suggests classifying when a non-trivial virtual knot can be a connected sum of two trivial virtual knots. The nearby sentences add the crucial hidden assumptions that connected sum for closed virtual knots is not well defined, while the long-knot version is well defined and ordered, and that the long-knot closure problem is only described as closely related, not equivalent. Earlier context in Section 2.3 defines the natural closure map from long virtual knots to oriented compact virtual knots and notes that the parts of the Kishino knot close to unknots. Section 5.2 also supplies an explicit example showing that such a phenomenon really occurs, so your draft is close but should be tightened to the paper's exact wording and logical strength.
